> On Feb 24, 2015, at 2:05 AM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>
> Hi Michael,
>
> Well, this is clearly the direction to go.
>
> One question: how would stan::services work with PyStan/RStan when those
> interfaces want to provide initialization data directly (e.g., without
> referencing a file)? It was this situation that led me to think about
> JSON in the first place.
>
> I'm also not clear on the callback approach -- Does RStan use that
> approach anywhere? Returning a pair or throwing an exception makes sense
> to me in this case.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Allen
>
> On 02/23, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> stan::services::argument_parser basically does this already
>> -- it accepts a string of flattened arguments, checks their
>> validity, and returns an informative error on failure.  The idea
>> is that once command has been refactored any of the
>> interfaces can call it by provided call backs to handle things
>> like output and error messages.  This assumes that we
>> use the hierarchical argument structure, which is very much
>> unsettled amongst the developers.
>>
>> On Feb 23, 2015, at 11:59 AM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>>
>>> Bob,
>>>
>>> I'd be happy to help out with this effort. Not knowing that much about
>>> previous efforts to do this kind of thing in C++ projects, my initial
>>> thought was to have a function like:
>>>
>>> int stan::gm::marshal_stan_args(json_string, empty_stan_args)
>>>
>>> with Stan throwing an exception if it doesn't work. (C++ exceptions are
>>> easy to handle in Python.) Alternatively, à la stan::gm::compile
>>>
>>> int stan::gm::marshal_stan_args(&std::cerr, json_string, empty_stan_args)
>>>
>>> but I'd rather have explicit feedback to the interface about an error
>>> than simply writing to std:cerr and returning -1. The main reason for
>>> this is that some of these new web-based interactive environments (like
>>> IPython notebook) do not really have std:cerr. Perhaps it could return
>>> json with information about success or failure? Or populate another
>>> struct like StanArgsError? (If only C++ could return multiple
>>> arguments!)
>>>
>>> Thanks,
>>>
>>> Allen
>>>
>>> On 02/23, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>> We absolutely need to do something along these lines to
>>>> get rid of all the duplicate code.
>>>>
>>>> I believe Daniel and Michael are slowly working their way
>>>> toward that kind of design, though maybe with some code
>>>> object rather than something like JSON.
>>>>
>>>> The big question in my mind is how to write the interfaces
>>>> on the language side so that the calls look idiomatic from
>>>> Python, R, etc.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
>>>>
>>>> P.S.  In case you need a JSON parser, Mitzi and I wrote one as
>>>> part of Stan that works with callbacks (like a SAX parser
>>>> for XML).    Using the one in Boost looked like a huge pain
>>>> and I enjoy writing parsers.  Nobody's ever plumbed it through,
>>>> but we were planning to allow it as an alternative data format
>>>> for initialization and data.
>>>>
>>>>> On Feb 23, 2015, at 1:43 PM, Allen B. Riddell <a...@ariddell.org> wrote:
>>>>>
>>>>> Hi everyone,
>>>>>
>>>>> Here's a proposal for a change to the PyStan/RStan/CmdStan interface
>>>>> that would eliminate a lot of code duplication. It also happens to be an
>>>>> easier change than any of the proposed Stan 3.0 API changes
>>>>> (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/Interfaces-3.0-Spec). I'd
>>>>> welcome any comments.
>>>>>
>>>>> ---
>>>>>
>>>>> Sampler and optimizing parameters (e.g., adapt_gamma, stepsize_jitter,
>>>>> ...) are gathered and validated by RStan, PyStan, and Stan using nearly
>>>>> identical code. It would be advantageous if checking to see if
>>>>> parameters make sense occurred in one place in the Stan C++ library.
>>>>> Interfaces (RStan/PyStan/etc) could provide a set of arguments to Stan,
>>>>> Stan could validate the arguments and then return a coherent StanArgs
>>>>> instance (or throw an informative exception). This change would require
>>>>> modest changes to existing code.
>>>>>
>>>>> RStan provides an example of what the StanArgs class might look like in:
>>>>> rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan/stan_args.hpp.
>>>>>
>>>>> One challenge is that (de)serializing C++ classes directly is impossible
>>>>> because C++ lacks reflection. On the other hand, there are some JSON libraries
>>>>> out there, including one that's built from Boost, that would make the work of
>>>>> constructing an instance easier. In this scenario, PyStan/RStan would submit a
>>>>> prepared set of arguments for validation in JSON. CmdStan might even use this
>>>>> interface directly since command-line arguments are already strings.
>>>>>
>>>>> For some additional background, here's an example from PyStan and RStan of
>>>>> duplicated code (stan_fit.hpp):
>>>>>
>>>>> ```
>>>>> if (model.num_params_r() == 0 && algorithm != Fixed_param) {
>>>>> throw std::runtime_error("Must use algorithm=\"Fixed_param\" for model that has no parameters.");
>>>>> }
>>>>> ```
>>>>>
>>>>> and CmdStan:
>>>>>
>>>>> ```
>>>>> if (model.num_params_r() == 0 && algo->value() != "fixed_param") {
>>>>>  << "Must use algorithm=fixed_param for model that has no parameters."
>>>>> ```
>>>>>
>>>>> The main reason to consolidate validation of arguments is that keeping track of
>>>>> default values (when the user doesn't provide a value for, say,
>>>>> `stepsize_jitter`) in 3+ different places creates a situation where it's easy
>>>>> for a developer to make a mistake and to have one interface fall out of sync
>>>>> with the others.
>>>>>
>>>>> Thanks,
>>>>>
>>>>> Allen
>>>>>
>>>>> p.s. Estimate of the lines of code dealing with validating sampler/optimizing arguments:
>>>>>
>>>>> 3% of lines of code in `rstan/rstan/R`
>>>>> 25% of lines of code in `rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan`
>>>>> 6% of lines of code in `pystan/*.py`.

messages.subject: GP experiment
messages.body_plain: I wanted to do the leukemia GP survival model in BDA3 with Stan, and first started experimenting with the following simpler GP classification model, which also shows how I would like to define GPs by combining basic covariance functions. With 250 data points Stan gives high N_eff, but sampling is very slow (N_eff/s<1.7e-02 and 5.5 hours to get total of 200 saved iterations from 4 chains (for comparison MML estimate with GPstuff takes less than 1.5s)). With 1000 data points I run out of memory in my laptop (using top, I can see the process going over 5GB before dying (for comparison MML estimate with GPstuff takes 45s, and less than 1GB memory)). Comaprison to MML with GPstuff is not fair, but I was still surprised that Stan for GP is so slow and that running out of memory with 1000 data points. We have had discussion on things which could make GPs faster in Stan. Feel free to use this example for testing (sorry for not including R code, and I guess the Matlab code would not be so useful for you).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
messages.body_plain:
Hey Aki,

I played with GP models in Stan a bit about a year ago (though with regression instead of classification).  The one major thing that is likely slowing this down is the call to cholesky_decompose which, for a matrix of even modest size, will be painfully slow.  Have you tried writing the model with f as the unknown and f ~ multi_normal(0,C) instead of z ~ normal(0,1)?  I suspect that this will make evaluating and differentiating the log likelihood much faster, though it may make curvature worse for sampling.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 24, 2015 at 11:07:25 PM UTC-5, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> @Marcus: sure, cholesky_decompose can be slow, but what's happening
> under the hood with multi_normal? There's no way around inverting the
> matrix C and calculating its log-determinant, right? (And this is
> often done with Cholesky...)

For a fixed precision matrix, it can avoid calculating the determinant and then the kernel of the multivariate normal is just a quadratic form, which Marcus has optimized a lot. And even if you input a fixed covariance matrix, I think it caches the Cholesky factorization, so the speed hit might be less noticeable.

For an unknown covariance matrix, there is not much in Stan now to avoid brute forcing a Cholesky factorization in vars. A lot of precision matrices in situations like this have the property that many of the off-diagonal elements approach zero. So, it might be possible to parameterize a precision matrix where those off-diagonal elements that approach zero are actually truncated to zero and then we might be able to utilize sparse algorithms. Another possibility is to parameterize the Cholesky factor of the covariance matrix, which would obviate the need to do a Cholesky decomposition of a covariance matrix. I haven't really looked into this either, but the first column of a Cholesky factor is a simple function of the first column of the covariance matrix it corresponds to. So, if you set the first column of the Cholesky factor according to the covariance function you have chosen, possibly the remaining below-diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor would fall into line conditional on that even if they were just unrestricted. You probably would have to do something clever about the diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor though.

There is an issue on GitHub for initializing the mass matrix, but I don't think it has been implemented yet.

Ben

On Monday, February 23, 2015 at 10:13:39 AM UTC-5, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> How about Tomi's version?
> From http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/diabcvd/wei_hs.stan

I'm seeing about the same thing. To summarize for these data (attached),
With the literal horseshoe prior in terms of a normal scale-mixture, NUTS doesn't converge. Basically, there is a funnel problem
With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but literal Cauchy priors on the positive parameters, NUTS does OK. But there are a few divergent transition even after the warmup period. This looks akin to the funnel-reparameterization example.
With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but indirect Cauchy priors on the positive parameters (using the Cauchy inverse CDF to transform the standard normal CDF of a priori standard half-normal), NUTS blows up for some chains and returns parameter values on the order of 10^20.
With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but indirect Cauchy priors on the positive parameters (using the ratio-of-half-normals approach), NUTS seems to yield reasonable posterior draws but there are a lot of divergent transitions
With the Tomi-trick horseshoe prior, NUTS again seems to yield reasonable posterior draws but there are a lot of divergent transitions

We talked about this briefly with Mike at the Stan meeting today. Without any data, the last three should be fine because the priors amount to products of independent standard normals (or some inverse gammas in Tomi's parameterization). But with the data, the posterior distribution is less amenable to NUTS than the prior distribution.

One issue might be that a horseshoe prior may not reasonable for an intercept, since there is no obvious reason to concentrate prior beliefs about it near zero. But even if I center the outcome variable, the above holds. Another issue might be that some prior is needed on the standard deviation of the errors, but I have tried a Jeffreys prior and a exponential prior for that without success.

Under the ratio of half-normals approach to tau, you get this pairs plot (with non-divergent transitions below the diagonal and divergent transitions above. It seems that for small (but not too small) values of the denominator, there is a concentration of divergent transitions that coincides with above average values of lp__. I think this suggests that the curvature near the mode along this dimension is great while the curvature is minimal away from the mode, and thus NUTS cannot adapt well.

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-yqtZ7ACD11s/VO15doPyg1I/AAAAAAAAAoc/yRWxnbEqY_c/s1600/pairs.png>

Thus, I think we need to see if this is a more general issue with situations like this before we recommend that horseshoe priors be used in something like stan_lm, particularly if we are not expecting users of stan_lm to do much in the way of diagnostics.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
> When I was debugging something like this, one thing I was surprised by
> was that for fixed hyperparameters it ran very quickly, even though I
> had not removed the costly linear algebra steps (i.e. calculate C at
> each sampling step, calculate Cholesky). To me this suggests that the
> curvature was bad for sampling, but maybe I'm not thinking about this
> correctly. Anyone have intuition about that?

GP likelihoods as a function of the hyperparameters are notoriously nasty,
with lots of saddle points that make optimization (and sampling) hard.
I think this is particularly bad when trying to do ARD with a squared-
exponential kernel.  Hyperpriors are critical here.

> Is there any support yet for initializing the mass matrix (aka the
> metric) for HMC? When I was last trying to debug this I found some
> chains that ran really quickly while others took forever (on the same
> data) and the mass matrix that was learned for each was pretty
> different. Not sure the chains that ran fast were actually giving good
> answers, but at least they ran.

My guess is that this is a manifestation of the nasty likelihood geometry
(different initializations lead to chains exploring different local
neighborhoods).

"Not sure the chains that ran fast were actually giving good

answers, but at least they ran.”  This is a great way to upset anyone
who takes MCMC seriously.  I jest, but in all seriousness slow but
diagnostic of pathologies is infinitely better than fast and ignorant.

> I feel like there should be some
> connection between the mass matrix and the covariance C, but I went to
> look in the literature to see if anyone had explored this (e.g.
> Radford Neal didn't say much about what mass matrix he used in the
> original HMC + GP work) and didn't find anything.

Nope, there’s no immediate connection.  The GP covariance defines
the correlation of points in data space, not the hyperparameters space
from which we sample.

> What exactly gets plotted in the divergent transitions case?  Is it
> just where the parameters started before running into numerical
> issues?  Or where they wind up if there was some progress in half
> the binary tree when there was a divergence in the second half?
>
> Given how far a single transition can move in HMC, neither of these
> may be very informative to where the values were at just before
> the divergent step.

Once a divergence is detected the tree building stops and the
current sample is returned — that sample could be from anywhere
in the tree built up to that point.

The difference between the sampled point and the points that
actually diverged is something to be weary of, but given how
concentrated the divergent samples are here I think it’s safe
to say that we’ve identified the pathological region.

> A side question for Michael:  why are these called "divergent"?
> I believe it means we get non-finite values (NaN, +inf, -inf) on
> the unconstrained scale, which can mean +inf or -inf on the
> constrained scale, but not necessarily (e.g., positive constrained
> -inf values mean underflow to 0 on the constrained scale).

Technically a divergence is defined not as the state reaching infinity
or NaN but rather the state diverging away from the true level set.
This is diagnosed as the change in Hamiltonian exceeding the
sampled slice, log_u + max_delta.  The relevant code is

            double h = this->hamiltonian_.H(this->z_);
            if (boost::math::isnan(h))
              h = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();

            util.criterion = util.log_u + (h - util.H0) < this->max_delta_;
            if (!util.criterion) ++(this->n_divergent_);

> but I went to

Radford used alternating conditional sampling for latent values and hyperparameters. The approach for estimating the mass matrix for hyperparameters is described in the appendix of his book Bayesian Learning for Neural Networks and in the technical report Monte Carlo implementation of Gaussian process models for Bayesian regression and classification. It's based on expected/conditional second derivatives of the density so that these don't depend on the actual value of the hyperparameters.

Aki

messages.body_plain:
Aki and Mike, regarding the mass matrix:

The leukemia example Aki sent is with a non-Gaussian observation model
(Bernoulli + logit) so in addition to the hyperparameters we've got
1000 latent parameters f which are highly correlated, and in fact we
know the correlation between them, it's given by the GP's covariance.

Neal [1997, p. 16] uses Gibbs sampling for the latent values, not HMC.

Seth

> attached

>> issues that were resolved when I just told Stan to only save a few
>> parameters of interest (rather than entire covariance matrices). Is
>> this option available in MatlabStan?
>
> I made the model so that it's not saving covariance matrices. And the memory problem happens right in the beginning before anything is stored.
>
>> but I went to
>> look in the literature to see if anyone had explored this (e.g.
>> Radford Neal didn't say much about what mass matrix he used in the
>> original HMC + GP work) and didn't find anything.
>
> Radford used alternating conditional sampling for latent values and hyperparameters. The approach for estimating the mass matrix for hyperparameters is described in the appendix of his book Bayesian Learning for Neural Networks and in the technical report Monte Carlo implementation of Gaussian process models for Bayesian regression and classification. It's based on expected/conditional second derivatives of the density so that these don't depend on the actual value of the hyperparameters.
>
> Aki

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
messages.body_plain:
The reason why cholesky_decompose is a lot slower than you think (vs multi_normal) has to do with the way autodiff works.  Basically, the slowest part of evaluating the log probability with Stan is creating autodiff variables.  A new one has to be created for every "elementary" operation that is performed on a parameter.  For instance, this is the reason that vectorization is such a big win, not because there can be fancy SIMD instructions under the hood, but because there are far fewer autodiff variables created.  This is also a big part of the reason that fixing the hyperparameters makes it much faster, because then the kernel matrix is no longer a parameter and doesn't need to be autodiff'd.

cholesky_decompose is particularly slow because it is literally autodiffing through all the operations of a cholesky decomposition.  This results in a MASSIVE number of autodiff variables (O(N^3) for an NxN covariance matrix) being created which takes far longer than just the basic Cholesky factorization of the underlying matrix.  In contrast, multi_normal has been fairly heavily optimized and specialized such that evaluating it creates only O(N) autodiff variables.  If someone was motivated, they could even bring that down to O(1).

So, in short, yes, multi_normal uses the Cholesky decomposition under the hood, but it does so in a far more efficient way than cholesky_decompose() is (or likely ever will be) able to.

Anyway, hope this helps clarify things a bit.  It's possible that the improved curvature behaviour of the Matt trick improves sampling enough that the speed gains of using multi_normal aren't worth it or are a wash, but I somewhat doubt it.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
This is interesting, the interaction between modeling choices and computation.

> On Feb 25, 2015, at 2:29 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> On Monday, February 23, 2015 at 10:13:39 AM UTC-5, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> > How about Tomi's version?
> > From http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/diabcvd/wei_hs.stan
>
> I'm seeing about the same thing. To summarize for these data (attached),
> With the literal horseshoe prior in terms of a normal scale-mixture, NUTS doesn't converge. Basically, there is a funnel problem
> With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but literal Cauchy priors on the positive parameters, NUTS does OK. But there are a few divergent transition even after the warmup period. This looks akin to the funnel-reparameterization example.
> With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but indirect Cauchy priors on the positive parameters (using the Cauchy inverse CDF to transform the standard normal CDF of a priori standard half-normal), NUTS blows up for some chains and returns parameter values on the order of 10^20.
> With the Matt-trick horseshoe prior but indirect Cauchy priors on the positive parameters (using the ratio-of-half-normals approach), NUTS seems to yield reasonable posterior draws but there are a lot of divergent transitions
> With the Tomi-trick horseshoe prior, NUTS again seems to yield reasonable posterior draws but there are a lot of divergent transitions
>
> We talked about this briefly with Mike at the Stan meeting today. Without any data, the last three should be fine because the priors amount to products of independent standard normals (or some inverse gammas in Tomi's parameterization). But with the data, the posterior distribution is less amenable to NUTS than the prior distribution.
>
> One issue might be that a horseshoe prior may not reasonable for an intercept, since there is no obvious reason to concentrate prior beliefs about it near zero. But even if I center the outcome variable, the above holds. Another issue might be that some prior is needed on the standard deviation of the errors, but I have tried a Jeffreys prior and a exponential prior for that without success.
>
> Under the ratio of half-normals approach to tau, you get this pairs plot (with non-divergent transitions below the diagonal and divergent transitions above. It seems that for small (but not too small) values of the denominator, there is a concentration of divergent transitions that coincides with above average values of lp__. I think this suggests that the curvature near the mode along this dimension is great while the curvature is minimal away from the mode, and thus NUTS cannot adapt well.
>
>  <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-yqtZ7ACD11s/VO15doPyg1I/AAAAAAAAAoc/yRWxnbEqY_c/s1600/pairs.png>
>
> Thus, I think we need to see if this is a more general issue with situations like this before we recommend that horseshoe priors be used in something like stan_lm, particularly if we are not expecting users of stan_lm to do much in the way of diagnostics.
>
> Ben
>

> On Wednesday, February 25, 2015 at 6:52:46 PM UTC+2, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> > The reason why cholesky_decompose is a lot slower than you think (vs multi_normal) has to do with the way autodiff works.  Basically, the slowest part of evaluating the log probability with Stan is creating autodiff variables.  A new one has to be created for every "elementary" operation that is performed on a parameter.  For instance, this is the reason that vectorization is such a big win, not because there can be fancy SIMD instructions under the hood, but because there are far fewer autodiff variables created.  This is also a big part of the reason that fixing the hyperparameters makes it much faster, because then the kernel matrix is no longer a parameter and doesn't need to be autodiff'd.
> >
> >
> > cholesky_decompose is particularly slow because it is literally autodiffing through all the operations of a cholesky decomposition.  This results in a MASSIVE number of autodiff variables (O(N^3) for an NxN covariance matrix) being created which takes far longer than just the basic Cholesky factorization of the underlying matrix.  In contrast, multi_normal has been fairly heavily optimized and specialized such that evaluating it creates only O(N) autodiff variables.  If someone was motivated, they could even bring that down to O(1).
> >
> >
> >
> > So, in short, yes, multi_normal uses the Cholesky decomposition under the hood, but it does so in a far more efficient way than cholesky_decompose() is (or likely ever will be) able to.
> >
> >
> > Anyway, hope this helps clarify things a bit.  It's possible that the improved curvature behaviour of the Matt trick improves sampling enough that the speed gains of using multi_normal aren't worth it or are a wash, but I somewhat doubt it.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
messages.body_plain:
There are two things that I can imagine happening here.  One, the curvature of the problem may be hard; given the nature of the model it could have a funnel like structure.  (it's not exactly that because the funnel would be distorted by the   RMHMC could help us here if it was ready but alas...

The other possibility, which the variability between chains somewhat suggests, is that the random initialization is performing really badly here.  Providing a well constructed initialization may help a lot and get you the best of both worlds.  For instance, randomly draw the kernel parameters (s_sexp, l_sexp, s_linear, s_constant), evaluate the kernel matrix C and then draw f ~ multi_normal(0,C) to construct the initialization.

This a case where having an initialization block (something we've talked about) would help a LOT so that you wouldn't have to reimplement your kernel functions outside the Stan model to produce the initialization.  An init block for a model like this would be maybe three lines of code...if we had support for that.

Cheers,
Marcus
.

> > > The reason why cholesky_decompose is a lot slower than you think (vs multi_normal) has to do with the way autodiff works.  Basically, the slowest part of evaluating the log probability with Stan is creating autodiff variables.  A new one has to be created for every "elementary" operation that is performed on a parameter.  For instance, this is the reason that vectorization is such a big win, not because there can be fancy SIMD instructions under the hood, but because there are far fewer autodiff variables created.  This is also a big part of the reason that fixing the hyperparameters makes it much faster, because then the kernel matrix is no longer a parameter and doesn't need to be autodiff'd.
> > >
> > >
> > > cholesky_decompose is particularly slow because it is literally autodiffing through all the operations of a cholesky decomposition.  This results in a MASSIVE number of autodiff variables (O(N^3) for an NxN covariance matrix) being created which takes far longer than just the basic Cholesky factorization of the underlying matrix.  In contrast, multi_normal has been fairly heavily optimized and specialized such that evaluating it creates only O(N) autodiff variables.  If someone was motivated, they could even bring that down to O(1).
> > >

messages.body_plain:
I've thought that the Cholesky thing I'm using is the multivariate version of the non-centered parameterization. Using that removes part of the funnel.

I initialized everything to 0 on unconstrained scale. Intializing the latent values to 0 is a good choice for GPs. Covariance function parameters could be intialized better, but zero on unconstrained scale is not a bad choice. The default random sampling is really bad for GPs.

I did not look at the memory usage when not using Cholesky, because it was so far from producing anything useful.

My only concern is that GitHub's https addresses make it more difficult to source .R files. For example, if we park Andrew's CRAN-incompatible stan() function in a stan.R file under http://mc-stan.org, then it can be sourced with the regular source() function that comes with R. If that file is under some https://github thing, then you have to do devtools::source_url(), which means the person has to have the devtools package installed. That is not too big a deal, but it is an additional hurdle.

One possibility would be to have a progress report after 5% of the warmup is done, then after 50% of the warmup, then after all the warmup.  Each time it could give a rough estimate of when it would be done.  (A rule of thumb could be that warmup takes 2/3 of the time, so we could take the time after 5% of warmup and multiply it by 30, then we could take the time after 50% of the warmup, then we could take the time after 100% of the warmup and multiply it by 1.5.  Maybe with a default setting that if the first time lag (after 5% of the warmup) is less than 1 second, it suppresses the output.

A

On Thursday, February 26, 2015 at 10:44:46 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I have to say, that beep is very satisfying.
>
> Would it make sense for there to be the option of just a little bit of progress-report output so that the user knows when it’s half done, etc?  I’m torn on this:  the old rstan output was too much, and I prefer the current less-verbose option.  But for a long computation it’s frustrating to not have progress report.

The parallel chains plus RStudio makes it such that I don't know how to do it. On Windows, the chains start in their own R process and nothing comes back to the main process until they are done. You can write to stdout or stderr but it doesn't flush to the main process until the end, so that is pointless for a progress report. On not Windows, you can see stdout in real time if you work in a terminal. But then you have all the chains writing to stdout simultaneously and it is a giant mess. I sometimes only output the progress of chain 1, but sometimes chain 1 finishes before the last chain even starts and it looks to the user like a freeze. Furthermore, it seems as if most people are using RStudio now and they don't direct stdout to the Console.

I think we would have to do something complicated like pass an R environment with an R progress bar to C++ and have the C++ update the progress bar.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] GP experiment
messages.body_plain:
Seth asked in email, but I'll answer here
> Hey Aki, you have HMC in GPStuff, right? How's it compare on this or
> other examples? And are there any important differences between your
> implementation and what Stan's doing?
>
> Any theories about why the samples from the model without Cholesky are
> so terrible?

When using HMC or NUTS in GPstuff, the sampling is made alternating the sampling of the latent values given the covariance function and likelihood parameters and the sampling of the covariance function and likelihood parameters given the latent values. The sampling of the latent values uses an approximative posterior covariance to create a transformed latent space (corresponding to using a mass matrix). This approximative posterior covariance combines the prior covariance and an approximative likelihood contribution. This transformation makes a big difference in the sampling efficiency. Since the transformation is conditional on the fixed covariance function and likelihood parameters, the transformation is fixed during the latent value sampling, and thus there is no need to compute the gradients through the Cholesky. Both these conditional samplings are fast, but the dependency between latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters makes the overall mixing slow, but not as slow as Stan without Cholesky. Without Cholesky there are really strong dependencies between latent values and a funnel when combined with sampling of the covariance function parameters at the same time. With Cholesky the sampling in Stan is efficient, it's just that computation of Cholesky and autodiffing through Cholesky makes it slow and use a lot of memory as Marcus explained.

Recently, instead of HMC/NUTS I've used combination of elliptical slice sampler and surrogate slice sampler (which samples both the latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters at the same time with a GP specific algorithm), which seems to produce better overall mixing speed.

Sampling for GP models has been studied a lot, and based on all that and my own experiments, I think that HMC/NUTS/RHMC is not going to be fast for sampling both latent values and the covariance function and likelihood parameters. These recent Stan experiments seem to provide additional evidence for that.

To get fast GPs in Stan, the integration over the latent values should be made using Laplace's method (or EP).

Aki

messages.subject: CRAN update
messages.body_plain:
CRAN only required minor changes for rstan, so we should be able to take care of that very soon.

One of the issues was that g++-4.9 emits

warning: 'long long' is a C++11 extension [-Wc++11-long-long]

due to #including

goodrich@T540p:/opt/stan$ git grep -F -n "long long" src/stan | cat
src/stan/agrad/rev/var.hpp:160:      var(unsigned long long n) :
src/stan/agrad/rev/var.hpp:170:      var(long long n) :
src/stan/io/dump.hpp:76:      void write_val(const unsigned long long int& n) {
src/stan/io/dump.hpp:92:      void write_val(const long long& n) {

Why are these long long if we are not using C++11 yet? I could change these in the StanHeaders R package without us having to release a new version of Stan, but I wanted to make sure that the long longs were not essential. If they are, then rstan can be compiled in C++11 mode, but then we would not be able to build a binary with the llvm-g++-4.2 compiler on older versions of the Mac operating system.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
That's really awesome.

Some feature requests/questions, in no particular
order or priority:

1. The posterior summary stats is wasting a lot of
horizontal space (super premium on the web) for the
control.  Is there some way to minimize that when it's
not being used?  Maybe put it above or below the plot?

2.  When you trim the number of entries in the table,
it'd be great to have the trim be for containers.

A nice option might be to have each parameter unfold
or collapse, as in a standard hierarchical file browser.
Then the trim might be how many to show when it's expanded.
I doubt anyone's going to have enough named parameters that
including them all is problematic.

3.  For tables of numbers, there should always be right
alignment so the decimal places line up if possible.  Nothing's
going to solve the parameters with different scales problems
other than scientific notation throughout.

4. The show/hide customization thing on the parameters plot
is hard to see.  I think we'll need conventions as to where
these general controls go.  For something this general, not
having it on the display itself makes sense to me if that's
possible.

5.  I didn't understand the "ALL theta_raw" vs. "theta_raw"
option, even after poking at it a bit.  "theta_raw" seems to
be a synonym for "theta[1]"?

6.  The greyed out names under the table don't seem to
work as controls, even thought they look like they'll be
editable because they pop up cursors.  I don't see the point
of having those.  I changed the 50% to "44%" and got "no records
found".  Then after I did that, nothing works at all.  So maybe
a "reset table" option would be helpful.  I went into view
table options and changing decimal places reset everything --- this
is probably not what you want to happen in general.  Destructive
ops with no "back" button need strong warnings to users, maybe
in the form of a modal dialog box.

7.  I don't know what First/Previous/Next/Last are for.
They look like live buttons but can't be clicked.

8.  In the search box, what am I supposed to be searching for?
It looks like I can enter parameters?  If I select "mu_raw"
and get just that, then edit the box on the bottom, it needs
to be one of the ones I'm viewing, which seems confusing.

9.  What does the "Estimate" control at the top do?  It doesn't
seem to do anything when I click it, yet it looks like something
clickable.  The diagnose options are really sweet.  I like that
you can customize the warning levels.   The glossary's really
awesome, too.

10.  Andrew has told me time and time again not to use "samples"
when I mean "draws".  A sample is a collection of draws.  I've
almost broken myself of the habit, but it's tough, because a whole
lot of the literature conflates "sample" and "draw".  The "effective
sample size" is the effective size of the sample.  A pure MC
sample has an effective sample size of the number of draws.
So the label should maybe be "effective sample size / draws" or
"n_eff / iterations" --- run it by Andrew and let him decide.

11.  The summary of sample parameters is fantastic.  Maybe an
option to include sd or intervals would make it even fantasticker.

12.  How do you set the maximum lag for the correlation plots?
Oh, I see --- you've got customization for everything.  That's
really cool.  I still think the customization should be a bit more
front-and-center rather than in small text to the right.  Maybe
in the same control box as the one that lets you enter parameter names.

- Bob

For the Stanbox, sure, let’s think big, but for plain old Stan in R, I think a progress report after 5% of the warmup is done, then after 50% of the warmup, then after all the warmup, would be fine.  The key is to give a rough sense of timing.  Actually, just 2 progress reports, one after 5% of warmup, and one after 50% of warmup, I think that should do it.

> On Feb 27, 2015, at 10:16 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> It might be possible to spawn a separate process that reads the
> progress and reports in some kind of standalone GUI.  What
> I'd really like is 4 parallel progress bar if we're running
> four chains, each with an estimated time to finish that's
> continually updated as (avg time per iteration * number of
> iterations left).  It'll usually overestimate remaining time
> because warmup iterations take long, so maybe a rolling average
> would be better.
>
> Seems like a lot of work, though.
>
> The right thing to do as Ben suggests is to run in threads where
> we can easily control inter-thread communication within a single
> process using semaphores and locks.
>
> I don't think we should have something that requires user input to finish.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>> On Feb 28, 2015, at 2:57 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> On Thursday, February 26, 2015 at 10:44:46 PM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> Would it make sense for there to be the option of just a little bit of progress-report output so that the user knows when it’s half done, etc?  I’m torn on this:  the old rstan output was too much, and I prefer the current less-verbose option.  But for a long computation it’s frustrating to not have progress report.
>>
>> I put in a very hackish version that writes the progress to a file every 500 iterations and opens the file if you are in interactive mode. You have to refresh to see subsequent progress. It is annoying for programs that finish before you even have time to look at the file.
>>
>> Ben
>>

> Ben

messages.body_plain:
I filed an issue:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1316

I'm about to go fix it now.  Shouldn't take long at all.

I believe we put it in to deal with 64-bit Windows compilers,
which treat "size_t" as synonymous with "unsigned long long", rather
than "unsigned long" like the Unices (Linux/Mac).  We can't have
both "size_t" and "unsigned long" due to ambiguity, and we didn't
know how to work around it before.

We're better at C++ now, and I think I can just use Boost's enable_if
mechanism to restrict to primitives without running afoul of
Windows issues.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Can we just drop MSVC support now that we have g++
working?  Then we could presumably get rid of this
file.

Does MSVC use different sizes than g++?

Which compiler and bit size are we using on Jenkins?

What's required for CRAN?

If I just leave everything alone with "long long", what
are the consequences?

Does someone else understand Boost fixed-size types or
the built-in fixed size macros well enough to help me out?

What I need is the following constructors for agrad::var:

  var()
  explicit var(vari*);
  var(double);

What I want is to have every arithmetic type use the
var(double) constructor, but there are conflicts with
unsigned long and vari*, despite var(vari*) being explicit.

Yes, I can get enable_if working on my Mac to pick out
arithmetic types, but I can't get it to work on Windows, so
tests fail on Jenkins.

Previously, we just used all of the following
constructors:

  var()
  explicit var(vari* vi)
  var(float), var(double), var(long double)
  var(bool), var(short), var(int), var(long), *** var(long long) ***
  var(unsigned short), var(unsigned int), var(unsigned long), *** var(unsigned long long) ***

The built-in types don't run into overload conflicts with each
other, but as soon as you get into the typedefs like size_t, uint64_t,
etc., the shit hits the fan when trying to overload.

The problem is that "long long" missed the boat for C++, so is only
in C++11.

Does using long long run afoul of CRAN policy.

The memory models in play are these:

                ILP32   LP64    LLP64
char             8       8       8
short           16      16      16
int             32      32      32
long            32      64      32
long long       64      64      64
size_t          32      64      64
pointer         32      64      64

ILP32:  32-bit Windows
LP64:   64-bit linux & mac
LLP64:  64-bit windows

I can't for the life of me figure out how to get the right set of
constructors to cover all inputs and not run into conflicts without
using long long.  And it looks like we can't get 64-bit integers
on ILP32 wihtout long long.

We could just punt altogether on long support in autodiff.
I think that'd require some serious test rewriting, and would be
less than ideal for third parties, but I think it may come to that.
We don't need it for running Stan models.

- Bob

Someone on stan-users gor MSVC to work with a more recent Boost, so I think dropping MSVC support would be a last resort.

> Does MSVC use different sizes than g++?

Probably not for MSVC >= 2012, which is what works with Boost

> Which compiler and bit size are we using on Jenkins?

Not MSVC

> What's required for CRAN?

Not MSVC; see

http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_flavors.html

> If I just leave everything alone with "long long", what
> are the consequences?

Would have to compile rstan in C++11 mode and thus not have a Snow Leopard binary.

> Does someone else understand Boost fixed-size types or
> the built-in fixed size macros well enough to help me out?

No but maybe

> Does using long long run afoul of CRAN policy.

Without compiling in C++11 mode, yes.

> We could just punt altogether on long support in autodiff.
> I think that'd require some serious test rewriting, and would be
> less than ideal for third parties, but I think it may come to that.
> We don't need it for running Stan models.

I could patch the files that use long long for the StanHeaders package. However, that would slightly undermine the API if someone wanted to use StanHeaders in C++ mode. At this time, I think C++11 for rstan is not quite the right choice because we haven't done enough testing with how all the other code gets compiled.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Bob:
As an R user I do not like dozens of lines of output.  One or two lines is ok, but not 40 or so, which is the current default.  This fills up my R console and makes it hard for me to see what’s going on.  On the other hand, no output is a problem when the program takes a long time.  That’s why I like the idea of a progress bar or some sort of low-tech solution such as ETA based on 5% of warmup and 50% of warmup.
A
